content: The majority of individuals with epilepsy generally have a favorable prognosis, with their seizures being effectively managed using a single antiepileptic drug. However, approximately 30% of patients develop drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly those with focal seizures. This review focuses on the use of zonisamide as an add-on therapy for focal epilepsy that remains uncontrolled despite treatment with one or more antiepileptic drugs. It is an updated version of a Cochrane review initially published in 2018. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and tolerability of zonisamide as an adjunctive treatment for individuals with focal epilepsy who have not achieved adequate seizure control with other antiepileptic medications. For the most recent update, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web) and MEDLINE Ovid databases as of September 2019. Additionally, the authors reached out to Eisai Limited, the manufacturer and licensee of zonisamide, as well as experts in the field, to identify any ongoing or unpublished studies. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared zonisamide as an add-on therapy to either placebo or another antiepileptic drug in patients with focal epilepsy that was not adequately controlled by one or more concomitant antiepileptic drugs. Two independent reviewers selected the trials for inclusion, extracted data, assessed the risk of bias using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool, and evaluated the certainty of the evidence using the GRADE approach. The primary outcome was defined as achieving at least a 50% reduction in total seizure frequency. Secondary outcomes included tolerability and adverse effects. An intention-to-treat approach was employed for the primary analyses, and summary risk ratios (RRs) were calculated for each outcome. A 'Summary of findings' table was used to present the estimates of effects and the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. No new studies were identified since the previous version of the review. Eight studies, involving a total of 1636 participants, were included from earlier versions of the review. The pooled risk ratio (RR) for achieving at least a 50% reduction in seizure frequency with zonisamide at doses of 300 mg to 500 mg/day compared to placebo was 1.90 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.63 to 2.22; 7 trials, 1371 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). For any dose of zonisamide (100 mg to 500 mg/day), the RR was 1.86 (95% CI 1.60 to 2.17; 7 trials, 1429 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The number needed to treat (NNT) for one additional beneficial outcome was six (95% CI 4.1 to 6.8). Two trials provided evidence of a dose-response relationship for this outcome. The RR for treatment withdrawal due to adverse effects with zonisamide at doses of 300 mg to 500 mg/day compared to placebo was 1.59 (95% CI 1.18 to 2.13; 6 trials, 1099 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). For doses of 100 mg to 500 mg/day, the RR was 1.44 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.93; 6 trials, 1156 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The number needed to treat for one additional harmful outcome was 15 (95% CI 9.3 to 36.7). Adverse effects that were more frequently associated with zonisamide compared to placebo included ataxia (RR 3.85, 99% CI 1.36 to 10.93; 4 trials, 734 participants; low-certainty evidence), somnolence (RR 1.52, 99% CI 1.00 to 2.31; 8 trials, 1636 participants; moderate-certainty evidence), agitation (RR 2.35, 99% CI 1.05 to 5.27; 4 trials, 598 participants; low-certainty evidence), and anorexia (RR 2.74, 99% CI 1.64 to 4.60; 6 trials, 1181 participants; low-certainty evidence). Across the eight studies, the risk of bias was generally rated as low or unclear, except for two studies that were judged to have a high risk of attrition bias. Five of the eight studies were sponsored by the pharmaceutical companies that manufacture zonisamide. In conclusion, moderate-certainty evidence suggests that zonisamide, when used as an add-on therapy for individuals with focal epilepsy that is not controlled by one or more antiepileptic drugs, is more effective than placebo in reducing seizure frequency by at least 50%. However, the review was unable to determine the minimum effective dose or the maximum tolerated dose of zonisamide. The included trials only evaluated a maximum stable-dose phase of 18 weeks, so the long-term efficacy of zonisamide in controlling seizures remains uncertain. Furthermore, the findings cannot be generalized to monotherapy or to individuals with other types of seizures or epilepsy syndromes.
